source: Zheng, Huang, Mu, Hu, Lai (2024) Selective Modulation of Fear Memory in NREM Sleep (Adv Sci, mice)
finding: In mice, replaying the fear cue during non-slow-wave NREM weakened fear consolidation, but replaying it in slow-wave sleep strengthened it. Sleep substage decides the sign. Silencing frontal association cortex pyramidal cells removed both effects.
numbers: Abstract only: no N or effect sizes extracted. Calcium imaging: CS in SWS raised activity of fear-conditioning-active (FC+) neurons, correlated with freezing.
quote: TMR during slow wave sleep (SWS) enhances fear memory in mice.
limits: Mouse data; abstract read, full text not opened. The earlier mouse NREM weakening (Purple 2017) is therefore substage-dependent, not general.
agent_relevance: Same cue, opposite sign by state: gate any replay pass by an explicit state tag, and test sign of effect, not only size.

source: van der Heijden, van der Werf, van den Heuvel, Talamini, van Marle (2024) TMR to augment treatment in PTSD (Curr Biol)
finding: In PTSD patients, closed-loop TMR with the EMDR click as cue (after one EMDR session) raised slow-oscillation and spindle activity and reduced avoidance during script-driven imagery more than sham.
numbers: TMR n=17, sham n=16. Stimulus-locked SO and spindle increases correlated with symptom reduction in the TMR group. Only avoidance reduction was reported as clinical difference in the abstract.
quote: These data provide first proof of principle that TMR may be a safe and viable future treatment augmentation strategy for PTSD.
limits: Small N, proof of principle, authors hold a patent on the device. Positive direction in humans for a therapy memory, not for fear extinction per se.
agent_relevance: A cue attached to a corrected memory, replayed later, helped. Analogue: cue the corrected version of a belief, not the original error.

source: Xia, Chen, Zeng, Yao, Liu, Qin, Paller, Torres Platas, Antony, Hu (2024) Aversive memories weakened during sleep via reactivation of positive interfering memories (PNAS)
finding: Humans learned 48 word-aversive-image pairs, then positive images for half the words. NREM cues for both aversive and positive pairs weakened aversive recall and raised positive intrusions versus no cueing.
numbers: 48 nonsense words; abstract gives no N or effect size. Theta power after cues predicted positive recall; drift-diffusion modelling showed faster evidence toward positive judgments.
quote: cueing weakened aversive memory recall while increasing positive memory intrusions.
limits: Abstract only. Weakening works through interference from a competing memory, not through cueing the old memory alone.
agent_relevance: Replay can lower an old item if a newer competing item is replayed with it. This is the interference cost to neighbours (gap 4) used on purpose.

source: Biol Psychol (2026) Enhancing the suppression of unwanted memories during NREM sleep (Think/No-Think plus TMR)
finding: Re-presenting the 'suppress' instruction tone in NREM increased later suppression-induced forgetting versus uncued pairs. Cue raised theta and lowered spindle-slow-oscillation up-state coupling; only the coupling reduction predicted worse retrieval.
numbers: Abstract gives no N.
limits: Abstract only. Shows a replayed instruction (not the content) can change the fate of an item.
agent_relevance: Cue can carry a control instruction (suppress or keep), not only the memory. Fits a tag on stored items saying drop or keep.

source: Klaassen and Rasch (2024) Difficulty in artificial word learning impacts TMR (eLife)
finding: Auditory TMR in NREM improved overnight memory for easy-to-learn artificial words but had no effect on difficult words. Slow-wave density rose for both; nested spindle power was higher only for easy words.
numbers: N=22 healthy adults, within-subject. Abstract gives no effect size.
quote: TMR of the easy words improved their overnight memory performance, whereas TMR of the difficult words had no effect.
limits: Difficulty here is phonotactic, i.e. encoding depth, which may differ from weak-memory strength. It conflicts with the claim that the hardest items benefit most.
agent_relevance: Replay may not rescue items that were barely encoded. Gate replay to items with a minimal trace, not all failures (gap 3).

source: JSR (2026) Odor-cued targeted reactivation was unable to selectively benefit declarative memories during sleep
finding: Odour-cued reactivation of one of two object-location sets in NREM gave no overall benefit for the cued set over the non-cued set. An encoding-strength-dependent effect appeared. Odours caused a sustained (~15 s) drop in sigma power.
numbers: N=32 (18 women, 14 men), 2 sets of object locations, one odour per set.
quote: Our results show no overall benefit for the cued set over the non-cued one.
limits: Authors suggest benefit may have spread across the whole learning context. Contradicts item-specific selectivity.
agent_relevance: A cue may lift a whole context, not one item. Item-specific recall gains need a design that checks neighbours (gap 4).

source: JSR (2026) Concurrent presentation of memory-related odours and sounds nullified sleep reactivation benefits
finding: Sound cues gave a recall benefit only for weakly encoded memories. When sounds came together with odours tied to Remember or Forget instructions, the benefit was lost: both odours disrupted sound-induced reactivation.
numbers: Nap design; abstract gives no N or effect size. Odours also cut sigma power (12-16 Hz) for at least 10 s after offset.
quote: Sound cues produced a selective recall benefit for weakly encoded memories.
limits: Abstract only. Odour linked to multiple episodes interfered. This is a direct interference result for multi-cue replay.
agent_relevance: Do not stack several cues or tags on one replay pass; extra associated material can cancel the benefit. Weak-item gating is supported.

source: Neuropsychologia (2025) No evidence for a TMR effect on word-meaning priming
finding: Replaying homonym cues in a ~2 h nap gave an overall priming effect but no extra benefit from TMR on priming or on context recall, even though cues raised spindle/beta power versus control cues.
numbers: 80 homonyms, 40 primed; 40 cues replayed in nap plus 20 new control cues. N not in abstract.
limits: A physiological response without a behaviour gain. Linguistic material may be a boundary condition.
agent_relevance: Evidence that cue triggers processing and cue helps can come apart; measure the outcome, not the trace of processing.

source: Neuropsychologia (2025) Effects of targeted reactivation on memories cued once or multiple times during a nap
finding: No significant benefit for cued objects whether the sound was played once or five times. Sigma power predicted gains only for objects cued five times; post-sound delta power predicted gains for single cues.
numbers: N=31; 60 object-sound pairs; 40 cued (20 once, 20 five times), 20 uncued; an interference task raised error rates sharply.
limits: The interference task may have masked the effect. Confirms dose (cue count) did not buy gain.
agent_relevance: More repeats of a replay did not help at equal item count; spend tokens on selection, not repeats.

source: NPJ Sci Learn (2024) TMR with sleep disruption does not weaken week-old memories
finding: Cues that disturbed sleep did not weaken week-old object-location memories, unlike fresh memories in an earlier study. Memory becomes resistant to reactivation harm over time.
numbers: 74 object locations learned, cues for 50% delivered one week later in sleep. N not in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Age of the memory is a boundary condition for harm.
agent_relevance: Interference cost from replay is largest for fresh, unconsolidated items. Test harm on recent entries first (gap 4).

source: Imaging Neurosci (2025) Disarming emotional memories using TMR during REM sleep
finding: Re-presenting tones in REM reduced fMRI responses in the salience network and left amygdala and reduced heart-rate deceleration at 48 h. Arousal ratings fell for more upsetting images and rose for less upsetting ones.
numbers: Image-sound pairs, half cued in REM; N not in abstract.
limits: Physiological measures, not memory accuracy. Rating shift is item-dependent, i.e. regression toward the middle.
agent_relevance: Replay can change charge or confidence rather than content; a replay pass may recalibrate, not only store.

source: Sleep Adv (2025) TMR during REM sleep may selectively enhance the late positive potential (pilot)
finding: Odour cueing in REM raised late positive potential for old negative images only. It did not change memory performance, arousal or valence ratings.
numbers: N=16 (mean age 22.5). LPP 500-800 ms.
limits: Authors call it a pilot. Odour itself (phenylethyl alcohol) is a confound.
agent_relevance: Consistent with REM cueing not helping recall (Hu: REM g=-0.06).

source: Yuksel et al. (2025) Both slow wave and REM sleep contribute to emotional memory consolidation (Commun Biol)
finding: In a nap, TMR in REM impaired emotional memory. TMR benefit in SWS correlated with the product of time in REM and SWS. Emotional items gained more from TMR than neutral ones.
numbers: Abstract gives no N or effect sizes.
quote: Contrary to our hypothesis, reactivating emotional stimuli during REM impairs memory.
limits: REM impairment is a counterexample to REM null; stage mixes may matter.
agent_relevance: Stage effect can be negative, not just null: a replay in the wrong state can cost.

source: Shin, Kweon, Oh, Lee (2025) Personalized TMR enhances consolidation of challenging memories (NPJ Sci Learn, peer-reviewed version)
finding: The arXiv preprint is now published. Adjusting cue frequency to retrieval performance and task difficulty reduced memory decay and improved error correction under challenging recall versus plain TMR and control.
numbers: Three groups (personalized TMR, TMR, control), word-pair task. Group Ns not in abstract; arXiv version had t22=3.96.
quote: personalized protocol significantly reduced memory decay and improved error correction under challenging recall.
limits: Still one lab; no independent replication found in the 2024-2026 PubMed listing (first 50 of 175 TMR records scanned by title). Counter-evidence d05 and d06 on difficulty.
agent_relevance: Dose adapted to difficulty is a testable arm: equal total cue budget, allocated by item error rate versus uniform.

source: JSR (2025) Promoting vocabulary learning during sleep at home using closed-loop TMR
finding: Slow-wave-triggered cues at home raised translation accuracy for cued pseudowords (+8.6%) while uncued items fell (-4.6%).
numbers: N=24 adults, 40 pseudowords, half cued; Dreem 2 headband.
limits: Positive home study; same period has nulls (SleepStim home TMR, N=61). Percentages are test-retest changes.
agent_relevance: A cue-vs-uncue contrast in the same session is the unit to copy (within-agent control).

source: JSR (2026) Closed-loop TMR during sleep spindles enhances motor memory consolidation
finding: Cues triggered by detected spindles gave larger overnight gains for the cued motor sequence than for the uncued one. More cues landing in spindle trains gave larger gains; cues in isolated spindles gave smaller ones.
numbers: N=26; two 8-element sequences, within-subject; Portiloop device.
limits: Within-subject, single lab, abstract only. Skill memory, in line with Hu skill g=0.44.
agent_relevance: Timing relative to the system's own readiness (up-state, spindle) matters: replay when the agent is idle and unloaded.

source: Transl Psychiatry (2024) TMR during sleep improves emotional memory modulation following imagery rescripting (preregistered)
finding: Closed-loop home TMR with words from an updated memory made memories less vivid and less distressing than neutral or no-word controls.
numbers: N=80 healthy; 2-5 nights; imagery rescripting effects d=0.76-1.66; TMR gave extra gains. Preregistered.
limits: Authors are founders of the device company. Healthy sample. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Preregistered positive for cueing an updated memory.

source: PubMed listing of 'targeted memory reactivation' and 'meta-analysis' (read 2026-11-19)
finding: No new pooled TMR meta-analysis since Hu et al. 2020 turned up in PubMed. The meta-analysis query returned 3 records: two unrelated and Hu 2020. The plain TMR query returned 175 records.
numbers: 175 records for 'targeted memory reactivation'; first 50 scanned by title; 2024-2026 titles include at least 5 null or mixed reports (d06-d10).
limits: Title-level scan only; Europe PMC and Semantic Scholar APIs timed out or were rate-limited, so a pooled update was not computed. Preprints or non-indexed work may exist.
agent_relevance: The best pooled estimate for planning remains g about 0.13-0.29. Do not expect bigger from the newer literature.

source: Choi et al. (2026) IdleSpec: Exploiting idle time via speculative planning for LLM agents (arXiv 2605.22154)
finding: The paper re-runs Sleep-time Compute as a baseline in tool-using agents and says it relies on predictable future queries, which tool observations break. Sleep-time Compute used 13.7% of idle time on GAIA and sometimes scored below vanilla.
numbers: Average accuracy over GAIA and FRAMES (text table parsed, columns garbled): Gemma4-E4B vanilla 30.9, Sleep-time 31.0, IdleSpec 35.5; Qwen3.5-4B vanilla 33.2, Sleep-time 29.4, IdleSpec 40.0; Gemini-2.5-Flash vanilla 50.5, Sleep-time 50.1, IdleSpec 55.6. Seeds with +-std reported. Sleep-time prompt sensitivity: GAIA average 44.0-44.5% over three prompt variants.
quote: relies on the assumption of predictable future queries, which rarely holds when tool observations are inherently uncertain
limits: Authors compare against their own method and adapted the baseline's math prompt; row-to-model mapping from garbled table, check before quoting per-model numbers. Not equal-token: IdleSpec uses idle wall-clock time.
agent_relevance: Pre-computation that guesses the next question fails when the next observation is uncertain. Conditional plans (if A then X, else Y) survive uncertainty. This answers gap 7: benefit fades as predictability falls.

source: Samuel et al. (2026) Studying Without a Syllabus: task-agnostic environment preprocessing (arXiv 2609.10824)
finding: An agent that studies an environment before knowing the tasks beat no-study on 5 of 6 benchmarks. More study budget did not reliably help. Studied artifacts cut test-time sampling, and sometimes misdirected the solver.
numbers: Budgets $1, $5, $10, $25, $50: flat or non-monotonic on OfficeQA and Apex Agents; Harvey LAB meta-agent rose 0.271 to 0.348 (no archive) and 0.249 to 0.332 (archive). To beat the best studied Best@1, no-study needed 8 rollouts (BCP-G), 2, 3, 5, 2, 4 on the other five; those cost 1.6-5.5x as much. Archive: +0.046 mean where it helps, -0.021 where it hurts.
limits: Best@K for no-study assumes oracle selection, so crossovers are optimistic for no-study. Study cost vs test cost matched only through USD in Table 4.
agent_relevance: Equal-compute test exists here: study spend vs extra rollouts. Study helps, but extra study spend plateaus. Cap the idle pass.

source: Ye et al. (2026) Auto-Dreamer: learned offline memory consolidation for language agents (arXiv 2605.20616)
finding: A learned offline consolidator rewrites a region of the memory bank and beats fixed, RL and prompted memory baselines. Authors state no task is replayed and report no seed or task-order variance.
numbers: ScienceWorld: +7 points over best baseline with a 12x smaller active bank; ALFWorld: 6x less memory. Training adds +9.7 pp and +5.7 pp over the untrained pipeline on two domains, +1.0 pp on ALFWorld where it hurt the look_at_obj_in_light family. Consolidation cadence k in {1,5,20}: k=10 (ScienceWorld) beat both more and less frequent.
limits: Point estimates only (the paper says so). Layout of Table 1 garbled in text extraction, so per-baseline numbers were not copied. Consolidation is a rewrite, not cue-driven replay.
agent_relevance: Offline passes need a cadence: too frequent lacks evidence, too rare overloads context. Control for pass frequency at equal tokens.

source: Zou (2026) Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory (arXiv 2611.21648)
finding: A Claude agent rewrote its text memory each night from the day's transcript. The rewrite is the replay step. Corrupting the replay did not help transfer; wrong-detail corruption hurt recall, random text did not because the model filtered it.
numbers: 10 days x ~130,000 tokens; 30 runs (10 conditions x 3 histories). Multi-session recall 71+-7 with clean rewrite vs 0 with no rewrite. Recall 76 -> 60 with 40% detail corruption; random text paired difference 0+-2 at 40%. Overnight loss 8+-2 clean vs 21+-2 detail. SD across histories 5 points (clean).
limits: Single model, 3 histories; differences of 2 points or less are inside the SD. Memory size cap rises 19,500 to 117,000 tokens.
agent_relevance: Offline rewriting is a large win over no rewrite for cross-session questions; noisy replay is not a free gain. A replay step must not inject wrong detail.

source: Hu et al. (2026) ProAct: Anticipate and learn, idle-time compute in proactive agents (arXiv 2605.25971)
finding: An agent uses idle time to predict the user's next needs and gather evidence. On a 200-scenario benchmark with predictable need chains it cut required turns 14.8%, user effort 11.7%, and hallucination 28.1%.
numbers: ProActEval: 200 scenarios, 40 domains. Abstract numbers only; no token-matched control seen.
limits: Abstract and intro read. Benchmark was built with predictable need chains, so it favours the method (same caveat as sleep-time compute).
agent_relevance: Idle-time prep works when the next need is predictable by design. Matches the predictability condition in d19.

source: Singh et al. (2026) Librarian Agents: training LLMs to curate workspaces that anticipate future queries (arXiv 2610.22273)
finding: A builder agent precomputes a hierarchical file workspace before queries arrive and is trained by RL on downstream accuracy. It amortizes construction cost over repeated queries.
numbers: +33 percentage points over the strongest retrieval and precomputation baseline on BrowseComp-Plus; +31 point average on BRIGHT zero-shot.
limits: Abstract and intro read, results tables not extracted. RL-trained builder, not a prompt scaffold. Gains depend on many queries per corpus.
agent_relevance: Pre-computation pays only when its cost is spread over many later queries; count that in the token ledger.

source: Behrouz et al. (2026) Language Models Need Sleep (arXiv 2606.03979): variance and rehearsal-baseline check
finding: A text search of the full paper for seed, variance, standard deviation, confidence interval, and single-run found no reported variance. The listed baselines include SFT, GRPO and OPSD (see critique). No explicit replay-only or rehearsal-mix baseline was found in that search.
numbers: No numbers extracted this pass; earlier table: Qwen3-8B AIME-24 79.2 vs OPSD 76.6.
limits: Absence by text search is not proof; figures or appendix tables might hold error bars.
agent_relevance: Treat the 2.6-point margin as unverified until variance is shown (gap 9, still open).

source: Semantic Scholar citations of Sleep-time Compute (arXiv 2504.13171), 49 citing papers (read 2026-11-19)
finding: None of 49 citing papers by title tests an external token cue tied to a stored item as a replay trigger. Related titles: Lee et al. offline recurrence, Behrouz sleep, Auto-Dreamer, IdleSpec, ProAct, Studying Without a Syllabus, Librarian Agents, Can an LLM dream.
numbers: 49 citing papers listed, 13 flagged by the fetch tool as sleep, consolidation, idle compute or memory.
limits: Title-level screen only. arXiv API returned empty replies, so no direct keyword search on targeted memory reactivation could be run this pass; web search budget was exhausted.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open: the cue-bias design still has to be built.
